It is written for a human reader.","text":"At Vardnes, forty-seven-year-old Marit Solvang watched the sea swallow her mussel bucket at 13:09, fifty-one minutes before her grandmother Signe's tide table predicted. Signe had kept the table for forty years; Marit had never known it to fail. Lighthouse keeper Anders Holm's log recorded deviations beginning the previous July, growing from four minutes to nine, then twenty-two. Anders had left the lighthouse on March 2. His cottage key hung behind Marit's door; his barometer had remained at 1003 for a week. When seawater reached her shed, she moved the outboard into the loft. A dead gull lay below the breakwater.

Her brother Tomas would call from Bergen on Sunday. The ferry Kittiwake passed the point at 16:40 on Tuesdays and Fridays. Before dark, Marit took the log to Anders's cottage. Beneath his barometer she found a chart marking the lighthouse cellar and a warning: 'If the tide comes an hour early, do not open the lower door.' Three knocks sounded beneath the floor. A sodden paper slid between two boards. In Anders's handwriting it said, 'Check Signe's table.' Below was tomorrow's date.

At home, Marit found that date's tide times crossed out in Signe's faded ink. Her grandmother had written: 'This is when it starts knocking. It will use the hand of the last person who opened the door.' Marit laid the wet message beside the page without letting their edges touch.

Then the telephone rang. She answered but said nothing. Over the hiss of water, Anders whispered, 'Your grandmother didn't write that warning.' Marit gripped the receiver. 'Then who did?' The voice changed to Signe's. 'Bring the table down, Marit. I can't remember the next tide.'"}
